slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by framing linear algebra as a debugging language for graphics. The audience should see matrices not as tables of numbers, but as maps that move frames, areas, volumes, and normals. Emphasize that the source span is short, so the lecture favors geometric readings over encyclopedic algebra.

slides.title: Chapter Route
slides.notes: Use this slide as a map for the session. Point out that each later object depends on an earlier diagnostic: determinant first identifies collapse, matrix product explains composition, inverse solves or undoes, and decompositions reveal directions. This prevents the chapter from feeling like unrelated algebra facts.

slides.title: Determinants As Signed Size
slides.notes: Pause before writing formulas. A determinant is a measurement of the frame built by the columns. In two dimensions it tests triangle winding and area scale; in three dimensions it tests handedness and volume. This geometric reading explains why a zero determinant is a collapse, not just a bad denominator.

slides.title: Determinant Rules
slides.notes: The point of these rules is not memorization for its own sake. Scaling one vector scales the measured size, while sliding one side parallel to itself preserves the size. Those two pictures make determinant algebra feel inevitable and prepare students for Cramer ratios and determinant tests later.

slides.title: Matrices As Maps
slides.notes: Stress the column view because it is the most useful graphics mental model. When a vertex or direction vector is multiplied by a transform, its coordinates choose a linear combination of transformed basis directions. This also clarifies why scale, shear, and rotation are visible in the columns.

slides.title: Matrix Product
slides.notes: Connect the abstract product to rendering practice. The row-column rule looks strange until it is tied to composition, because one composite matrix can transform many vertices. Make students say the order aloud: AB applied to x means B acts first, then A under the column-vector convention.

slides.title: Matrix Operations
slides.notes: This slide is a compact reference, but it should be taught as a collection of contracts. Identity is the do-nothing transform, transpose changes the viewpoint on the array, inverse is an undo operation, and determinant tells whether that undo operation can exist without degeneracy.

slides.title: Special Matrices
slides.notes: Move from left to right and ask what each structure buys. Diagonal matrices isolate axes, symmetric matrices provide clean orthogonal eigendirections, orthogonal matrices make inverse equal transpose, and singular matrices explain collapsed dimensions. These categories become shortcuts in graphics code and diagnostics.

slides.title: Cofactors
slides.notes: Explain that cofactors are a disciplined way to avoid losing signs. The checkerboard sign and the smaller determinant are conceptually simple, but the work grows quickly. That is why the lecture uses cofactors to understand inverses and Cramer rule, while still recommending robust numerical routines in real code.

slides.title: Inverses
slides.notes: Treat the adjoint formula as explanatory rather than as the recommended implementation. The determinant in the denominator says exactly what can go wrong: if the frame area or volume has vanished, no algebraic undo can recover the lost direction. Near-zero determinants should trigger suspicion even when a library returns numbers.

slides.title: Linear Systems
slides.notes: Present Cramer rule as a lens on coordinates. The unknown coordinate is an area or volume ratio, so the same determinant that tests invertibility appears in the denominator. This also explains why a collapsed or nearly collapsed frame creates ambiguous or unstable solutions.

slides.title: Eigenvectors
slides.notes: Make the invariant-line idea vivid. Most vectors turn under a transform, but an eigenvector stays on its line. The determinant equation appears because a nonzero vector can solve the shifted homogeneous system only when that shifted matrix is singular.

slides.title: Symmetric Diagonalization
slides.notes: The right-to-left reading is crucial. First rotate into the eigenbasis, then apply independent diagonal stretches, then rotate back. This slide should make diagonalization feel like a coordinate choice rather than a mysterious formula. The symmetry assumption is what gives the clean orthogonal basis.

slides.title: SVD
slides.notes: Use SVD as the generalization that remains geometrically honest when eigenvectors become inconvenient. A nonsymmetric matrix may shear the circle into an ellipse without a clean orthogonal eigenbasis. Singular vectors still give orthonormal input directions, nonnegative scale factors, and orthonormal output directions.

slides.title: SVD Diagnostics
slides.notes: The SVD is not just a decomposition; it is a diagnostic report. The product of singular values gives area or volume scale, and the ratio between largest and smallest singular values predicts sensitivity. This is why SVD language appears in robust graphics tools and geometry processing.

slides.title: Normals
slides.notes: This is the payoff slide for graphics. Positions and tangents are carried forward by the linear part of the transform, but normals encode the constraint of being perpendicular to the tangent plane. The inverse transpose is the transform that preserves that dot-product constraint after shear or nonuniform scale.

slides.title: Numerical Checks
slides.notes: Tie the lecture back to executable evidence without relying on the notebook images. Each invariant corresponds to a visual failure mode: wrong winding, reversed transform order, unstable solve, broken decomposition, or incorrect lighting normals. Students should leave with a habit of writing these checks alongside graphics experiments.

slides.title: Summary
slides.notes: Close by returning to the inspection-toolkit theme. The chapter is not asking students to love algebra in isolation; it is giving them tests for transform order, area scale, frame collapse, decomposition meaning, and normal correctness. Those tests will reappear in transformations, viewing, shading, and the graphics pipeline.
